question_text:
Let $z_{n}$ be the complex number defined as $z_{n}=\left(n^{2}+n+1\right)+\mathrm{i}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.\\
(a) (i) Find $\arg \left(z_{0}\right)$.\\
(ii) Write down an expression for $\arg \left(z_{n}\right)$ in terms of $n$.

Let $w_{n}=z_{0} z_{1} z_{2} z_{3} \ldots z_{n-1} z_{n}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.\\
(b) (i) Show that $\arctan (a)+\arctan (b)=\arctan \left(\frac{a+b}{1-a b}\right)$ for $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^{+}, a b<1$.\\
(ii) Hence or otherwise, show that $\arg \left(w_{1}\right)=\arctan (2)$.\\
(c) Prove by mathematical induction that $\arg \left(w_{n}\right)=\arctan (n+1)$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
subject: HL
explanation:
(a) (i) $z_{0}=1+\mathrm{i}$

$$
\arg \left(z_{0}\right)=\arctan (1)=\frac{\pi}{4}=45^{\circ}
$$


(ii) $\quad \arg \left(z_{n}\right)=\arctan \left(\frac{1}{n^{2}+n+1}\right)$\\
(b) (i) attempt to use the compound angle formula for tan

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tan (\arctan (a)+\arctan (b))=\frac{\tan (\arctan (a))+\tan (\arctan (b))}{1-\tan (\arctan (a)) \tan (\arctan (b))} \\
& =\frac{a+b}{1-a b} \\
& \Rightarrow \arctan (a)+\arctan (b)=\arctan \left(\frac{a+b}{1-a b}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

(ii) METHOD 1

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \arg \left(w_{1}\right)=\arg \left(z_{0} z_{1}\right)=\arg \left(z_{0}\right)+\arg \left(z_{1}\right) \\
& =\arctan (1)+\arctan \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\
& =\arctan \left(\frac{1+\frac{1}{3}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}\right) \\
& =\arctan (2)
\end{aligned}
$$

\section*{METHOD 2}

\begin{align*}
& w_{1}=z_{0} z_{1}=(1+\mathrm{i})(3+\mathrm{i})  \tag{M1}\\
& =2+4 \mathrm{i} \\
& \arg \left(w_{1}\right)=\arctan \left(\frac{4}{2}\right) \text { or labelled Argand diagram } \\
& =\arctan (2)
\end{align*}



(c) let $n=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { LHS }=\arg \left(w_{0}\right)=\arg \left(z_{0}\right)=\arctan (1)\left(=\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\
& \text { RHS }=\arctan (1)\left(=\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \text { so LHS = RHS }
\end{aligned}
$$


assume true for $n=k$, $\left(\right.$ so $\left.\arg \left(w_{k}\right)=\arctan (k+1)\right)$\\


\begin{align*}
& \arg \left(w_{k+1}\right) \\
& =\arg \left(w_{k} z_{k+1}\right)\left(=\arg \left(w_{k}\right)+\arg \left(z_{k+1}\right)\right)  \tag{M1}\\
& =\arctan (k+1)+\arctan \left(\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+(k+1)+1}\right)
\end{align*}


$=\arctan \left(\frac{(k+1)+\left(\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+(k+1)+1}\right)}{1-(k+1)\left(\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+(k+1)+1}\right)}\right)$\\
$=\arctan \left(\frac{(k+1)+\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}+3 k+3}\right)}{1-(k+1)\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}+3 k+3}\right)}\right)$\\
$=\arctan \left(\frac{(k+1)\left(k^{2}+3 k+3\right)+1}{\left(k^{2}+3 k+3\right)-(k+1)}\right)$



$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\arctan \left(\frac{k^{3}+4 k^{2}+6 k+4}{k^{2}+2 k+2}\right) \\
& =\arctan \left(\frac{(k+2)\left(k^{2}+2 k+2\right)}{k^{2}+2 k+2}\right) \\
& =\arctan (k+2)(=\arctan ((k+1)+1))
\end{aligned}
$$

since true for $n=0$, and true for $n=k+1$ if true for $n=k$, the statement is true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ by mathematical inductionR1

$h=\sqrt[3]{6}$

question_text: Use mathematical induction to prove that $\sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(n+1)!}$ for all integers $n \geq 1$. \\
subject: HL
explanation:
let $\mathrm{P}(n)$ be the proposition that $\sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(n+1)!}$ for all integers, $n \geq 1$ considering $\mathrm{P}(1)$ :


LHS $=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\mathrm{RHS}=\frac{1}{2}$ and so $\mathrm{P}(1)$ is true\\
assume $\mathrm{P}(k)$ is true ie, $\sum_{r=1}^{k} \frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(k+1)!}$\\
Note: Do not award $\boldsymbol{M} \mathbf{1}$ for statements such as "let $n=k$ " or " $n=k$ is true". Subsequent marks after this M1 are independent of this mark and can be awarded.\\
considering $\mathrm{P}(k+1)$ :\\
$\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} \frac{r}{(r+1)!}=\sum_{r=1}^{k} \frac{r}{(r+1)!}+\frac{k+1}{((k+1)+1)!}$\\
$=1-\frac{1}{(k+1)!}+\frac{k+1}{(k+2)!}$\\
$=1-\frac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+2)!}$\\
$=1-\frac{1}{(k+2)!}\left(=1-\frac{1}{((k+1)+1)!}\right)$\\
$\mathrm{P}(k+1)$ is true whenever $\mathrm{P}(k)$ is true and $\mathrm{P}(1)$ is true, so $\mathrm{P}(n)$ is true (for all integers, $n \geq 1$ )

question_text: Prove by mathematical induction that $5^{2 n}-2^{3 n}$ is divisible by 17 for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$. \\
subject: HL
explanation:
base case $n=1: 5^{2}-2^{3}=25-8=17$ so true for $n=1$

Note: The assumption of truth must be clear. Do not award the M1 for statements such\\
as "let $n=k$ " or " $n=k$ is true". Subsequent marks can still be awarded.

\section*{EITHER}
consider $n=k+1$ :\\
$5^{2(k+1)}-2^{3(k+1)}$\\
$=\left(5^{2}\right) 5^{2 k}-\left(2^{3}\right) 2^{3 k}$\\
$=(25) 5^{2 k}-(8) 2^{3 k}$\\
$=(17) 5^{2 k}+(8) 5^{2 k}-(8) 2^{3 k}$ OR $(25) 5^{2 k}-(25) 2^{3 k}+(17) 2^{3 k}$\\
$=(17) 5^{2 k}+8\left(5^{2 k}-2^{3 k}\right) \quad$ OR $25\left(5^{2 k}-2^{3 k}\right)+(17) 2^{3 k}$\\
$=(17) 5^{2 k}+8(17 s) \quad$ OR $25(17 s)+(17) 2^{3 k}$\\
$=17\left(5^{2 k}+8 s\right) \quad$ OR $17\left(25 s+2^{3 k}\right)$ which is divisible by 17

\section*{OR}
$\left(5^{2 k}-2^{3 k}\right) \times 5^{2}=5^{2 k+2}-25 \times 2^{3 k}=17 s \times 25$\\
$=5^{2 k+2}-8 \times 2^{3 k}-17 \times 2^{3 k}=17 s \times 25$\\
$=5^{2 k+2}-2^{3 k+3}-17 \times 2^{3 k}=17 s \times 25$\\
$=5^{2(k+1)}-2^{3(k+1)}-17 \times 2^{3 k}=17 s \times 25$\\
$=5^{2(k+1)}-2^{3(k+1)}=17 s \times 25+17 \times 2^{3 k}$\\
hence for $n=k+1: 5^{2(k+1)}-2^{3(k+1)}=17\left(25 s+2^{3 k}\right)$ is divisible by 17

\section*{THEN}
since true for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$,\\
therefore true for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$

Note: Only award R1 if 4 of the previous 6 marks have been awarded\\
Note: $5^{2 k}$ and $2^{3 k}$ may be replaced by $25^{k}$ and $8^{k}$ throughout.

This question asks you to explore some properties of the family of curves $y=x^{3}+a x^{2}+b$ where $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a, b$ are real parameters.

Consider the family of curves $y=x^{3}+a x^{2}+b$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$, where $a \in \mathbb{R}, a \neq 0$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.\\
First consider the case where $a=3$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.\\
(a) By systematically varying the value of $b$, or otherwise, find the two values of $b$ such that the curve $y=x^{3}+3 x^{2}+b$ has exactly two $x$-axis intercepts.\\
(b) Write down the set of values of $b$ such that the curve $y=x^{3}+3 x^{2}+b$ has exactly\\
(i) one $x$-axis intercept;\\
(ii) three $x$-axis intercepts.

Now consider the case where $a=-3$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.\\
(c) Write down the set of values of $b$ such that the curve $y=x^{3}-3 x^{2}+b$ has exactly\\
(i) two $x$-axis intercepts;\\
(ii) one $x$-axis intercept;\\
(iii) three $x$-axis intercepts.\\
\\
For the following parts of this question, consider the curve $y=x^{3}+a x^{2}+b$ for $a \in \mathbb{R}, a \neq 0$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.\\
(d) Consider the case where the curve has exactly three $x$-axis intercepts. State whether each point of zero gradient is located above or below the $x$-axis.\\
(e) Show that the curve has a point of zero gradient at $\mathrm{P}(0, b)$ and a point of zero gradient at $\mathrm{Q}\left(-\frac{2}{3} a, \frac{4}{27} a^{3}+b\right)$.\\
(f) Consider the points P and Q for $a>0$ and $b>0$.\\
(i) Find an expression for $\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2} y}{\mathrm{~d} x^{2}}$ and hence determine whether each point is a local maximum or a local minimum.\\
(ii) Determine whether each point is located above or below the $x$-axis.\\
(g) Consider the points P and Q for $a<0$ and $b>0$.\\
(i) State whether P is a local maximum or a local minimum and whether it is above or below the $x$-axis.\\
(ii) State the conditions on $a$ and $b$ that determine when Q is below the $x$-axis.\\
(h) Prove that if $4 a^{3} b+27 b^{2}<0$ then the curve, $y=x^{3}+a x^{2}+b$, has exactly three $x$-axis intercepts.\\

question_text:
This question asks you to explore some properties of polygonal numbers and to determine and prove interesting results involving these numbers.
A polygonal number is an integer which can be represented as a series of dots arranged in the shape of a regular polygon. Triangular numbers, square numbers and pentagonal numbers are examples of polygonal numbers.
For example, a triangular number is a number that can be arranged in the shape of an equilateral triangle. The first five triangular numbers are $1,3,6,10$ and 15 .
The following table illustrates the first five triangular, square and pentagonal numbers respectively. In each case the first polygonal number is one represented by a single dot.
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[scale=0.1,height=7cm]{SV_IBDP_FST_AA HL_May 2022_Paper 3_TZ1_1.png}
\end{center}
For an $r$-sided regular polygon, where $r \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}, r \geq 3$, the $n$th polygonal number $P_r(n)$ is given by
$$
P_r(n)=\cfrac{(r-2) n^2-(r-4) n}{2}, \text { where } n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+} .
$$
Hence, for square numbers, $P_4(n)=\cfrac{(4-2) n^2-(4-4) n}{2}=n^2$
\begin{parts}
\part[2] \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For triangular numbers, verify that $P_3(n)=\cfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. \hspace{3em} \item The number 351 is a triangular number. Determine which one it is. \end{enumerate}
\part[2] \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Show that $P_3(n)+P_3(n+1) \equiv(n+1)^2$.
\item State, in words, what the identity given in part (b)(i) shows for two consecutive triangular numbers.\;\hspace{34em}[1]
\item For $n=4$, sketch a diagram clearly showing your answer to part (b)(ii).\hspace{10em}[1]
\end{enumerate}
\part[3] Show that $8 P_3(n)+1$ is the square of an odd number for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
The $n$th pentagonal number can be represented by the arithmetic series
$$
P_5(n)=1+4+7+\ldots+(3 n-2)
$$
\part[3] Hence show that $P_5(n)=\cfrac{n(3 n-1)}{2}$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
\part[5] By using a suitable table of values or otherwise, determine the smallest positive integer, greater than 1 , that is both a triangular number and a pentagonal number.
A polygonal number, $P_r(n)$, can be represented by the series
$$
\sum_{m=1}^n(1+(m-1)(r-2)) \text { where } r \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}, r \geq 3 \text {. }
$$
\part[8] Use mathematical induction to prove that $P_r(n)=\cfrac{(r-2) n^2-(r-4) n}{2}$ where $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
\end{parts}

This question asks you to investigate conditions for the existence of complex roots of polynomial equations of degree 3 and 4.

& r=-\alpha \beta \gamma .
\end{aligned}
$$

\item Show that $p^2-2 q=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.
\item Hence show that $(\alpha-\beta)^2+(\beta-\gamma)^2+(\gamma-\alpha)^2=2 p^2-6 q$.
\end{enumerate}
\part[2] Given that $p^2<3 q$, deduce that $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ cannot all be real.
Consider the equation $x^3-7 x^2+q x+1=0$, where $q \in \mathbb{R}$.
\part[2] Using the result from part (c), show that when $q=17$, this equation has at least one complex root.
Noah believes that if $p^2 \geq 3 q$ then $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are all real.

\item By varying the value of $q$ in the equation $x^3-7 x^2+q x+1=0$, determine the smallest positive integer value of $q$ required to show that Noah is incorrect.\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;[2]
\item Explain why the equation will have at least one real root for all values of $q$.
\end{enumerate}
Now consider polynomial equations of degree 4 .
The equation $x^4+p x^3+q x^2+r x+s=0$, where $p, q, r, s \in \mathbb{R}$, has roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ and $\delta$. In a similar way to the cubic equation, it can be shown that:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& p=-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta) \\
& q=\alpha \beta+\alpha \gamma+\alpha \delta+\beta \gamma+\beta \delta+\gamma \delta \\
& r=-(\alpha \beta \gamma+\alpha \beta \delta+\alpha \gamma \delta+\beta \gamma \delta) \\
& s=\alpha \beta \gamma \delta .
\end{aligned}
$$
\part[1] \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Find an expression for $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2$ in terms of $p$ and $q$.\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;[3]
